- Model consistently underestimates prices in early forecast periods, especially after recent spikes.
- Forecasts tend to be too low in the first 5–10 days of the 30-day window, then gradually rise — suggesting a lag in capturing short-term momentum.
- Overshoots occur after sharp price spikes (e.g., 73+), where model predicts a peak that doesn’t materialize or overcorrects downward.
- Mean reversion is overemphasized — model often predicts a sharp drop after a peak, but actual prices stabilize or rebound.
- Forecasts for the last 5–10 days of the 30-day window are often too high, possibly due to overconfidence in recent trends or failure to account for seasonal or policy-driven corrections.
- Model exhibits persistent downward bias in the middle of the forecast horizon (days 10–20), likely due to underweighting of recent upward momentum.
- When history includes a recent high, model tends to forecast a lower peak or fails to anticipate a rebound — suggesting poor handling of “recovery” or “policy reversal” events.
- Forecasts should be adjusted upward if the 30-day history includes a recent spike above 70, especially if the spike is followed by a dip — model underreacts to such patterns.
- Model often fails to capture the “tail” of the distribution — i.e., it underestimates the probability of a sharp rebound or correction near the end of the forecast window.
